abstract.p: Cancer immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer treatment, offering durable responses in a subset of patients. Despite this progress, cancer cells have developed sophisticated mechanisms to evade immune surveillance, including genetic mutations, activation of immune escape pathways, alterations in the tumor microenvironment, and metabolic reprogramming. Additionally, the immune system’s ability to effectively target cancer cells can be compromised by immune tolerance and functional exhaustion. There is growing evidence that abnormal activation of cancer signaling pathways, such as the Wnt/β-catenin, Notch, JAK/STAT, p53, and PTEN pathways, acts independently or through crosstalk to form complex regulatory networks that influence tumor immune escape, the therapeutic response, and immune resistance. Consequently, elucidating the mechanisms by which these signaling pathways contribute to tumor immune escape is essential for optimizing current immunotherapy regimens and developing novel therapeutic strategies. Targeting these pathways in combination with immunotherapy represents a promising approach to overcome immune resistance and enhance treatment efficacy. The integration of pathway modulation with immunotherapeutic interventions may reveal new avenues for more effective and durable cancer treatments.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Since the mid-20th century, noncommunicable diseases, including cardiovascular diseases and cancer, have progressively supplanted communicable diseases as the primary contributors to premature mortality worldwide [1]. Current epidemiological trends suggest that cancer is poised to overtake cardiovascular diseases as the leading cause of premature death in this century [2]. It has taken significant effort to develop effective cancer treatments. Beyond conventional approaches such as surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, breakthroughs in genetic engineering and immunology have catalyzed the emergence of targeted therapies and immunotherapy, revolutionizing cancer treatment paradigms [3, 4].

Immunotherapy is a broad spectrum of therapies that control and eliminate cancers by reversing the immunosuppressive microenvironment of cancer patients and activating the immune response against cancer cells [3]. Cancer immunotherapy mainly includes immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), cell therapy, tumor vaccines, therapeutic blockade antibodies, small molecule inhibitors and immune system modulators, among which ICIs constitute the core of immunotherapy [5–7]. Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) was the first molecule shown to modulate the T cell response as a potential immune checkpoint molecule, pioneering ICIs therapy [8]. Cancer ICIs therapy works by inhibiting immune checkpoint molecules, thereby amplifying the immune system’s ability to target and destroy cancer cells [9–11]. Adoptive immunotherapy has also achieved significant breakthroughs in the treatment of hematological malignancies in recent years. For instance, anti-B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has shown both feasibility and safety in clinical trials for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma [12, 13]. Additionally, several therapeutic advances have effectively extended the median overall survival (OS) of cancer patients, contributing to more personalized and effective treatment strategies. Prominent examples include the humanized anti-human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) monoclonal antibody trastuzumab for breast cancer and talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) engineered herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) oncolytic virus (OV) for unresectable metastatic melanoma [14–16].

The core principle of cancer immunotherapy lies in restarting and sustaining the cancer-immune cycle, which encompasses a series of critical steps: the release of tumor antigens, tumor antigen presentation, the activation and proliferation of effector T cells, the migration of T cells to tumor sites, the infiltration of T cells into tumor tissue, and ultimately, the recognition and elimination of cancer cells. These processes are tightly regulated by a balance of positive and negative factors. Disruption at any stage of the cancer-immune cycle can serve as a rate-limiting factor, hindering the immune system’s ability to control cancer progression and significantly limiting the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy [17, 18].

The progressive accumulation of numerous point mutations and structural alterations in the genome drives the uncontrolled cell proliferation that fundamentally characterizes cancer as a genomic disease [3, 19]. While each cancer patient typically harbors hundreds to thousands of gene mutations, only a subset of these-known as driver genes-play a pivotal role in tumor initiation, progression, and the disruption of the cancer-immune cycle, thereby influencing the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy. Advances in DNA sequencing technologies and bioinformatics have significantly accelerated the identification of driver genes, which makes it difficult to characterize the function of these genes in a short period of time, especially their impact on the cancer-immune cycle and cancer immunotherapy [20]. Nevertheless, cancer driver genes often serve as critical components or regulators of oncogenic signaling pathways, creating intricate networks that modulate pathway activity. These oncogenic signaling pathways can significantly impact the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy by driving immune escape and drug resistance, regulating immunosuppressive molecule expression, impeding antigen processing and presentation, and modulating cytokine release and inflammatory responses [21–24].

In this manuscript, we highlight the critical role of oncogenic signaling pathways in tumor initiation and progression, review the advancements and current challenges in immunotherapy, and elaborate the impact of key cancer signaling pathways on cancer immunotherapy. This discussion enhances our understanding of the tumor microenvironment (TME), immune escape mechanisms, the physiological basis of immunotherapy, and the development of drug resistance. Furthermore, it offers valuable insights into the potential of personalized cancer therapy and the strategic design of combination therapies.

sec.title: The development and challenges of cancer immunotherapy
sec.p: The remarkable advances in cancer immunotherapy have revolutionized the field of oncology. However, its clinical efficacy remains inconsistent, and significant challenges persist. A major obstacle to broader success lies in the multifaceted nature of treatment resistance, among which dysregulated oncogenic signaling pathways play a critical role in facilitating both tumor development and immune evasion.

sec.title: The development of cancer immunotherapy
sec.p: As early as the 1950 s, researchers conducted pioneering experiments by transplanting liver cancer cells into the anterior ocular chamber, establishing a novel model for investigating the dynamic interplay between the human immune system and malignant cells [25]. In the 1970 s, researchers investigated how specific immune cells, including natural killer (NK) cells and T cells, functioned in cancer suppression [26, 27]. Since the late 20th century, extensive research and clinical trials have examined cancer immunotherapies including ICIs and CAR-T cell therapy, representing the modern application of the immune system to treat cancers [8, 28].

Molecular cloning technology enabled the large-scale production of purified cytokines, leading to the first Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of cytokine therapy for treating hairy cell leukemia [29]. Cytokine therapy represents an active form of nonspecific immunotherapy. High-dose aldesleukin (interleukin-2, IL-2), for instance, enhances cytotoxic activity of T cells and NK cells while promoting T cell differentiation and survival, thereby augmenting the body’s antitumor capacity [30, 31].

ICIs currently represent the most clinically effective form of cancer immunotherapy. Immune checkpoints constitute constitutively expressed regulatory pathways that maintain immune homeostasis by preventing excessive activation and autoimmunity. ICIs function as targeted therapeutic agents that block inhibitory signaling pathways on T cells - such as programmed cell death protein 1/programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) and CTLA-4 - thereby reactivating the body’s antitumor immune response. Within the TME, malignant cells hijack these checkpoint molecules to evade immune surveillance [6]. Following FDA approval of ipilimumab in 2011 as the pioneering ICI, the past decade has witnessed the clinical emergence of ICIs therapies, including CTLA-4 and PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors [32]. Taking PD-1/PD-L1 signal as an example, signal blockade prevents phosphorylation of the immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs (ITIM) and the immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motif (ITSM) on PD-1’s intracellular domain, thereby restoring T cell receptor (TCR) signaling through src homology 2 domain-containing phosphatase 1/2 (SHP-1/2) phosphatase inhibition relief. Concurrently, blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 signal amplifies CD28-mediated co-stimulation and reinstates T cell metabolic fitness and clonal expansion, substantially prolonging survival in advanced malignancies such as lung cancer, gastric carcinoma, and metastatic melanoma [9, 10, 33].

In addition, cell therapy represents another rapidly advancing approach in immunotherapy, primarily encompassing CAR-T-cell therapy, TCR-engineered T-cell therapy, adoptive tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy and NK cell therapy. Cell therapy is a precision medicine strategy that involves modifying or utilizing immune cells or tumor cells to specifically recognize and eliminate tumors. To date, the FDA has approved several CAR T-cell products, with CD19 remaining the predominant therapeutic target across these biologics [34]. Mechanistically, patient-derived T cells are genetically modified to express CAR, whose extracellular single-chain variable fragments (scFv) confer specific CD19 antigen recognition, enabling targeted elimination of CD19 + malignant cells [35]. Separately, the first TIL therapy, Amtagvi, has recently gained approval for advanced melanoma treatment [36, 37].

Beyond lymphocyte modification, scientists have engineered OV to selectively replicate in tumor tissues while maintaining attenuated virulence. These viruses lyse tumor cells, releasing tumor-associated antigens (TAAs), damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), cytokines, and chemokines. Collectively, these components act in synergy to robustly activate the body’s immune system, eliciting a powerful and targeted anti-tumor immune response [38–40]. In addition, tumor vaccines represent another promising form of immunotherapy, which function by activating the patient’s own immune system to recognize and eliminate tumor cells. They are broadly categorized into preventive and therapeutic vaccines. Prophylactic vaccines like the 9-valent human papillomavirus (9vHPV) vaccine can prevent approximately 90% of global cervical cancer cases. Therapeutic vaccines such as Sipuleucel-T employ autologous cellular immunotherapy targeting prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP), demonstrating significant OS benefits in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) patients (Fig. 1) [41–43].

A ICIs enhances anti-tumor immunity by blocking inhibitory pathways such as PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4/CD80-CD86 interactions, which releases T-cell suppression and restores immune surveillance against tumors. B Immune-mediated cytokine therapy enhances anti-tumor immune responses by stimulating the polarization of antigen-presenting cells, promoting the proliferation and activation of cytotoxic T cells and B cells, and facilitating the formation of lymphokine-activated killer (LAK) cells. C Adoptive cell immunotherapy harnesses ex vivo expanded or genetically engineered immune cells (e.g., CAR-T, TCR-T, or tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes) to enhance tumor recognition and elicit potent cytotoxic responses upon reinfusion into patients. D Cancer vaccine works by delivering tumor-specific antigens to activate helper T cells, and establish long-lasting anti-tumor immunity that targets and eliminates cancer cells. E OV therapy selectively infects and lyses tumor cells while stimulating systemic anti-tumor immunity through the release of TAAs, cytokines, DAMPs and PAMPs in the tumor microenvironment

sec.title: Current challenges in cancer immunotherapy
sec.p: Recent advances in cancer immunotherapy have made remarkable progress, with breakthrough efficacy demonstrated in areas such as PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, CAR-T cell therapy, and personalized vaccines, significantly prolonging survival in some advanced-stage patients [44, 45]. Nevertheless, cancer immunotherapy encounters several limitations. Primary among these is variable treatment responsiveness across cancer types, largely dictated by host immune competence. For example, it is difficult for cell therapy to penetrate the TME in solid cancers, resulting in significantly less effective treatment than in blood cancers [12, 13, 46–48]. Cancers such as melanoma, bladder cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) are generally more sensitive to immunotherapy. In contrast, abundant immunosuppressive cells and factors within the TME characterize pancreatic cancer (PC) and prostate cancer, leading to poorer immunotherapy outcomes [10, 49–52]. Moreover, tumor cells employ diverse immune evasion mechanisms to circumvent immune surveillance and develop immunotherapy resistance, a major determinant of suboptimal treatment efficacy and transient therapeutic benefits. Clinically, while the objective response rate to immunotherapy approaches 30%, a substantial proportion of initial responders eventually acquire resistance, leading to disease recurrence [36, 53, 54].

The mechanisms primarily involve the following aspects: (1) Acquired homozygous loss of beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) leads to decreased expression of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I on the surface of cancer cells, resulting in impaired tumor antigen presentation and TCR function [55]. Although downregulation of HLA-I may partially relieve the activation of inhibitory receptors on NK cells, tumor cells often evolve multiple countermechanisms in this dual immune context - enabling escape from both T cell- and NK cell-mediated immunity. Suitable NK cell-based therapeutic strategies remain to be developed [56, 57]. (2) Impaired editing and copy number loss of neoantigens during cancer progression direct immune escape [58, 59]. (3) During immunotherapy, increased infiltration of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), or increased release of inhibitory cytokines, collectively facilitate tumor immune evasion and T-cell dysfunction [60, 61]. (4) Elevated expression of immune checkpoint molecules, such as PD-1, CTLA-4, T-cell immunoglobulin domain and mucin domain-3 (TIM3), and lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG3) [6, 62, 63]. (5) Dysregulated signaling pathways impair T-cell effector functions. For instance, phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) deletion constitutively activates the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT) pathway, impairing CD8 + T cell infiltration and cytotoxic function [64]. Activation of the Wnt/catenin beta 1 (β-catenin) pathway induces immune desert by suppressing lymphocyte recruitment [65, 66]. Mutations in interferon-gamma receptors 1/2 (IFNGR1/2) or janus kinases 1/2 (JAK1/2) render the JAK-signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) pathway unresponsive to interferon-γ (IFN-γ) signaling, compromising this pivotal cytokine’s role in initiating and sustaining anti-tumor immunity (Fig. 2) [67].

B Immunosuppressive cells infiltrate tumors and secrete immunosuppressive factors, creating an immune-resistant microenvironment that blocks anti-tumor immunity. C Underexpression of HLA Class I on the surface of cancer cells leads to impaired tumor antigen presentation and TCR function. D Immunoescape is caused by reduced editing of neoantigens and copy number loss during tumor progression. E Upregulation of immune checkpoints leads to tumor immune evasion by suppressing T-cell activation and promoting exhaustion in the tumor microenvironment. F The interaction between aberrant tumor signaling pathways and the immune microenvironment drives tumor immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance

sec.p: Given the complex and extensive role of cell signaling pathways in tumor biology and therapy resistance, coupled with the transformative potential of cancer immunotherapy, this review examines how dysregulated signaling pathways modulate immunotherapy responses.

sec.title: Dysregulated oncogenic signaling pathways promote tumor development and suppress antitumor immune responses
sec.p: Cancer-associated oncogenic signaling pathways comprise intracellular molecular cascades that regulate growth, proliferation and survival. These pathways are crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis under physiological conditions. However, their persistent activation or inactivation - driven by genetic mutations, epigenetic modifications, or microenvironmental changes - can promote malignant transformation. This aberrant state features dysregulated proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, and increased metastatic potential [68–72]. For example, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations represent the predominant driver alteration in NSCLC patients [73]. Mutated EGFR continuously activates the PI3K/AKT, RAS/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), JAK/STAT pathways, promotes cell cycle progression, inhibits apoptosis, and induces the expression of immune escape related factors [74–77]. In addition, Aberrant oncogenic signaling is pivotal in maintaining tumor heterogeneity and plasticity. Colorectal cancer (CRC), a paradigm of tumor heterogeneity, frequently harbors mutations in adenomatous polyposis coli (APC), kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS), and tumor protein p53 (TP53) genes. Their spatiotemporal heterogeneity underpins the disease’s biological complexity [78, 79]. However, crosstalk between secondary EGFR mutations and MET proto-oncogene, receptor tyrosine kinase (c-MET) amplification or activation in NSCLC cooperatively promotes cancer stemness and confers resistance to EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) [75, 80, 81].

Oncogenic signaling pathways actively shape immunosuppressive microenvironments. Specifically, Wnt/β-catenin activation impairs dendritic cells (DCs) recruitment and maturation, consequently diminishing tumor antigen presentation [21, 82]. The transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGF-β) signaling pathway plays a central role in Treg cell biology by promoting Treg differentiation and function, inhibiting effector T cell activity, and facilitating tumor immune evasion [83]. Moreover, MYC proto-oncogene, bHLH transcription factor (MYC)-driven glutamine metabolism competes for the nutrient substrate required for T cell function, directly contributing to T cell depletion [84]. In addition, numerous studies report that oncogenic signaling pathways regulate the expression of immune-related factors and immune checkpoint molecules, helping tumors evade T-cell-mediated killing [64, 85, 86].

To date, inhibitors targeting oncogenic signaling pathways have achieved clinical success. However, the activation of mutations or bypass signals may contribute to the emergence of resistance. Investigating the role of oncogenic signaling pathways serves as a critical link bridging fundamental mechanisms and clinical translation. The analysis of signaling pathway networks offers a theoretical foundation for overcoming immunotherapy resistance and designing combination strategies that integrate targeted therapy with immunotherapy, representing a frontier in translational medicine research.

sec.title: Effects of major oncogenic pathways on the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy
sec.p: Aberrant activation of various oncogenic signaling pathways significantly modulates the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy. This section examines the impact of key pathways including Wnt/β-catenin, neurogenic locus homolog (Notch), JAK/STAT, loss of p53 function, loss of PTEN function, and other relevant signaling pathways on immune regulation and treatment outcomes.

sec.title: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway
sec.p: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is an evolutionarily conserved pathway that plays critical roles in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and adult physiological processes [87]. Furthermore, the β-catenin pathway critically regulates immunotherapy responses. The most established and significant effect of Wnt/β-catenin signaling on the TME is promoting immune desert phenotypes [65, 88, 89]. T-cell infiltration levels serve as a crucial predictor for cancer immunotherapy efficacy. Reduced T-cell infiltration impairs ICIs responsiveness, compromises CAR-T-cell therapy functionality, and diminishes tumor vaccine-mediated T-cell activation, all of which significantly impact patient treatment outcomes and survival prognosis [90–92].

Pan-cancer analysis of TCGA data demonstrated that 33.9% (3137/9244) of tumors exhibited non-T-cell-inflamed phenotypes with triple the β-catenin mutation frequency compared to T-cell-inflamed tumors. Notably, activated β-catenin signaling associated with non-T-cell-inflamed phenotypes in 28 of the 31 analyzed tumor types [88]. Analysis of 372 HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCCs) revealed nuclear β-catenin positivity in 14.3% of tumors, which correlated with reduced CD8 + TILs and lower PD-L1 expression [93]. Immunohistochemical analysis of 155 CRC specimens demonstrated that Wnt/β-catenin pathway activation strongly correlated with impaired T-cell infiltration, with high β-catenin-expressing tumor samples showing significantly reduced CD8 + T-cell recruitment [94]. In melanoma, comparative analysis of 91 T cell-excluded tumors versus 106 T cell-inflamed tumors revealed β-catenin signaling activation as the most prominent distinguishing feature. Strikingly, elevated β-catenin signaling was observed in 49% of tumors exhibiting T cell exclusion, compared to merely 4% of T cell-infiltrated lesions [95].

Therefore, understanding how Wnt/β-catenin signaling inhibits T-cell infiltration and developing corresponding interventions would facilitate the establishment of a T-cell-inflamed phenotype and enhance responsiveness to immunotherapy. DCs are essential for priming antigen-specific CD8 + T cells. Research demonstrates that mouse tumors with hyperactive β-catenin signaling exhibit a deficiency in CD103 + DCs. This deficiency was associated with reduced expression of key DC-related transcripts, including basic leucine zipper transcription factor, ATF-like 3 (BATF3), integrin alpha E, epithelial-associated (ITGAE), interferon regulatory factor 8 (Irf8), and thrombomodulin (THBD) [21, 95]. In addition, the β-catenin signaling pathway inhibits DC-recruiting chemokines, particularly C-C motif chemokine ligand 4 (CCL4) and C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 (CCL5), across multiple cancer types [21, 95–98]. Experimental studies demonstrate that hydrodynamic tail vein delivery of CCL5 in mice restores immune surveillance despite β-catenin pathway activation. Moreover, β-catenin signaling activation alone confers resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [21]. In human non-T-cell-inflamed tumor models, adoptive T-cell transfer therapy failed to rescue impaired T-cell priming due to CD103 + DC deficiency. This defect led to reduced C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 9/10 (CXCL9/CXCL10) production, consequently compromising CD8 + T-cell trafficking and infiltration [99]. In addition, the efficacy of immune-mediated cytokine therapy and OV therapy depend critically on the infiltration and activation of NK cells and T cells within tumor sites. However, β-catenin-mediated suppression of DC function and consequent T cell exclusion significantly undermine the therapeutic efficacy of these approaches [100, 101]. In cancers with activated β-catenin signaling, DCs exhibit promising yet incompletely realized therapeutic potential for orchestrating both immediate and sustained anti-tumor immune responses [102, 103].

Furthermore, the Wnt/β-catenin pathway impairs ICIs effectiveness by promoting the recruitment and persistence of immunosuppressive cells. Specifically, hyperactivated Wnt/β-catenin signaling in CRC recruits MDSCs to establish an immunosuppressive microenvironment [104]. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), Wnt/β-catenin signaling assisted in maintaining the M2 phenotype and immunosuppressive function of TAMs. Targeting TAM-mediated immunosuppression significantly enhances the efficacy of ICIs by boosting CD8 + T cell activity and suppressing MDSCs infiltration [105].

Beyond directly or indirectly modulating CD8 + T cell infiltration and function, β-catenin is reciprocally regulated by CD8 + T cells through feedback mechanisms that influence the signaling activity in cancer cells. Moreover, as scaffold proteins, axis inhibition protein 1/2 (AXIN1/2) form β-catenin degradation complexes by binding to APC, glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), and casein kinase I (CK1) via their multiple protein-interaction domains [87, 106]. AlkB homologue 5 (ALKBH5) demethylates AXIN2 mRNA, triggering its degradation upon dissociation from the N6-methyladenosine reader insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA binding protein 1 (IGF2BP1). This aberrantly activates Wnt/β-catenin signaling and upregulates dickkopf-related protein 1 (DKK1) to recruit MDSCs. Notably, both anti-DKK1 antibodies and ALKBH5-targeting small interfering RNA delivered by vesicular nanoparticles synergistically potentiate anti-PD-1 therapy in CRC [104].

Clinically, a subset of immunotherapy-refractory patients paradoxically exhibits accelerated tumor progression despite displaying remarkably elevated CD8 + T-cell infiltration and IFN-γ expression levels - termed ICIs-mediated hyperprogressive disease (HPD). This pattern is indistinguishable from that observed in complete responders. Mechanistic studies revealed IFN-γ-induced fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) upregulation in tumor cells drives oncogenic-metabolic crosstalk, enhancing β-catenin acetylation and promoting stemness reprogramming [107, 108]. Targeting the IFN-γ-FGF2-β-catenin signaling axis demonstrates efficacy in suppressing tumor progression in preclinical models.

Clinical and preclinical evidence demonstrates that the β-catenin pathway critically regulates tumor immune evasion and TME remodeling, suggesting that targeting its key components may provide considerable benefits in cancer immunotherapy [98, 109–112].

sec.title: The Notch signaling pathway
sec.p: The Notch gene encodes a family of highly conserved transmembrane receptors composed of extracellular and transmembrane subunits. Upon binding to adjacent cell ligands, Notch undergoes proteolytic cleavage to release the Notch intracellular domain (NICD), which translocates to the nucleus to regulate transcription [113, 114]. The impact of Notch signaling on immunotherapy efficacy is highly context-dependent. It can either promote immune evasion or enhance anti-tumor immune responses, depending on specific biological and microenvironmental conditions. In small cell lung cancer (SCLC) patients who benefit from immunotherapy, the Notch pathway is the most significantly enriched. Most Notch-associated genes show activated expression in these responders [115]. In contrast, preclinical studies reveal that triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) exhibiting Notch pathway hyperactivation shows limited response to ICIs alone, while combinatorial regimens incorporating Notch inhibitors markedly improve treatment outcomes [116, 117]. Retrospective studies further demonstrated that CRC patients with activated Notch signaling showed reduced disease control rates after ICIs treatment [118]. Understanding the role of Notch signaling mutations in shaping the TME and their underlying mechanisms may facilitate the discovery of biomarkers for identifying cancer patients likely to respond to immunotherapy.

At the molecular level, stromal cell engagement triggers PD-L1 expression in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) cells. A signaling axis involving Notch, c-MYC, and the enhancer of zeste homologue 2 (EZH2) mediates this effect. Therapeutic disruption of this synergistic pathway may facilitate the development of novel CLL-targeted immunotherapies [119]. In addition, concurrent activation of Notch and TGF-β pathways coupled with decreased immune cell infiltration (including T cells and NK cells) was observed in anti-PD-1-resistant CRC models. Local mRNA-based immunotherapy successfully restored PD-1 therapy sensitivity in these resistant tumors [120]. Clinical evidence demonstrates that Notch1/2/3 mutations correlate with sustained therapeutic responses in ICIs-treated NSCLC patients, showing improved objective response rates, prolonged progression-free survival (PFS) and OS. Notably, these patients exhibited higher metastatic burden compared to wild-type counterparts [121, 122]. Conversely, research in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) demonstrates that Trp53/cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2a (CDKN2A)/Notch1 triple-knockout organoids develop tumors exhibiting marked lineage heterogeneity and enhanced cellular plasticity [123].

Mechanically, Notch signaling establishes an immunosuppressive niche mainly by influencing macrophage polarization. Drug-resistant advanced LUAD samples exhibited high Jagged1/Notch1 expression, which promoted tumor M2-like TAM invasion. Notch signaling in basal-like breast cancer (BLBC) regulates the expression of the proinflammatory cytokines IL1β and C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2) to recruit TAMs. In contrast, Notch1 knockout in ESCC also induces T-cell depletion and M2-like differentiation of macrophages via the CCL2/C-C chemokine receptor type 2 (CCR2) axis [117, 123–125]. Furthermore, Notch pathway activation in macrophages directly regulates their differentiation. Recombination signal binding protein for immunoglobulin kappa J region (RBPJ) constitutes the principal transcriptional regulator of the Notch signaling pathway. Loss of RBPJ abrogates the differentiation of inflammatory monocytes into TAMs [126, 127]. In addition, the Notch signaling pathway critically governs the expansion and differentiation of MDSCs, thereby playing an essential role in regulating anti-tumor immune responses during immunotherapy [128–130].

Although the role of Notch signaling varies across cancer types, research confirms that sustained Notch pathway activity is essential for establishing, activating, and maintaining the optimal anti-tumor immune competence of T cells [131]. Conditional knockout mouse models demonstrate that Notch1/2 signaling enhances CD8 + T-cell proliferation and IFN-γ secretion, while conditional overexpression of NICD1 augments CD8 + T-cell cytotoxicity and granzyme B production [132]. Recent advances highlight the therapeutic potential of Notch signaling in T-cell immunotherapy. The efficacy of PD-1 blockade relies on CD28 co-stimulation, which is often deficient in exhausted T cells. However, studies demonstrate that lenalidomide-mediated activation of Notch signaling upregulates the expression of hes family bHLH transcription factor 1 (HES1), myelin protein zero like 2 (MPZL2), and T-box 21 (TBX21). This mechanism effectively restores anti-tumor responses to PD-1 inhibition in CD28-deficient murine models [133, 134].

In addition, engineered CARs enable targeted T-cell anti-tumor responses but face limitations due to scarce tumor-specific antigens and weak endogenous immunity. Synthetic Notch receptors overcome these limitations by enabling customized cytokine secretion, directing T-cell differentiation, and delivering novel therapeutic payloads. This approach achieves precision therapy through cross-induced antigen-specific receptor expression [135, 136]. Collectively, therapeutic targeting of Notch signaling combined with TCR- and CAR-based immunotherapies holds significant promise for advancing cancer immunotherapy, meriting substantial future research efforts.

sec.title: The JAK/STAT signaling pathway
sec.p: JAK and STAT proteins represent crucial intracellular signaling molecules that regulate diverse biological processes including cell proliferation, survival, differentiation, and immune responses. The JAK/STAT signaling pathway demonstrates ubiquitous activation across diverse cancer types. Notably, methylation-specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and microsatellite analysis of 80 HCC cases revealed constitutive JAK/STAT pathway activation in all examined tumor specimens [137]. Comprehensive clinicopathological analysis of 20 classical Hodgkin lymphoma cases with granulomatous reactions demonstrated that 50% of granulomatous lesions exhibited pSTAT3 positivity, potentially correlating with PD-L1 cellular expression patterns [138]. Diverse cytokines and growth factors trigger the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, which plays a pivotal role in modulating the TME and consequently influences both tumor immunosuppression and immunotherapy efficacy [139–141]. A Phase I clinical trial evaluating the combination therapy of a JAK inhibitor and anti-PD-1 antibody in Hodgkin’s lymphoma patients reported promising efficacy, achieving a best overall response rate of 53% (10/19 cases) [142]. Similarly, adjunctive therapy with a JAK1 inhibitor following anti-PD-1 treatment markedly potentiated anti-tumor immunity in patients with metastatic NSCLC [143].

The JAK/STAT pathway promotes immunotherapy resistance primarily by responding to T cell-derived IFN-γ and upregulating PD-L1. This cascade constitutes the core mechanism of IFN-γ-induced transcriptional immunosuppression [85, 144–146]. For instance, excessive IFN-γ activation in renal cell carcinoma (RCC) shapes a distinctive TME, featuring prominent lymphocyte infiltration coupled with JAK1/STAT1/PD-L1-mediated immunosuppressive mechanisms [146]. Furthermore, this signaling cascade is subject to negative regulation by the suppressor of cytokine signaling (SOCS) family, intracellular regulatory proteins that attenuate cytokine signal transduction through feedback inhibition. In RCC, EH domain-binding protein 1-like protein 1 (EHBP1L1) competitively binds to JAK1 at the SOCS1 interaction site, thereby blocking proteasomal degradation of JAK1.

In melanoma and CRC, transcriptional regulators SRY-box transcription factor 2 (SOX2) and steroid receptor coactivator-1 (SRC-1) suppress SOCS1/3 expression while activating JAK/STAT signaling, ultimately leading to PD-L1 upregulation [146–148]. Pharmacological suppression of SRC-1 activity or restriction of SOX2 expression may therefore enhance the therapeutic efficacy of PD-L1-targeted immunotherapy [147, 148]. Furthermore, the JAK/STAT signaling pathway plays a crucial yet dual role in IFN-γ-mediated anti-tumor immune responses. This functional duality primarily stems from the differential activation of STAT proteins, particularly STAT1 and STAT3, by IFN-γ. Such differential activation ultimately leads to distinct patterns of cytokine transcriptional activation [149, 150].

Additionally, a variety of cytokines and growth factors beyond IFN-γ modulate the JAK/STAT signaling pathway. (1) Studies have shown that interleukin-3 (IL-3) stimulation can restore proliferation and competitive capacity in human primary hematopoietic cells carrying RUNX family transcription factor 1 (RUNX1) deletion mutations. These mutations selectively enhance IL-3 receptor expression while suppressing JAK/STAT signaling, ultimately contributing to unfavorable outcomes in certain leukemia subtypes. The identification of RUNX1 mutation-driven reliance on the IL-3/JAK/STAT axis provides valuable insights for developing targeted therapeutic strategies [140]. (2) Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) has gained attention as an immunostimulatory agent in anti-tumor therapy. However, emerging evidence indicates that it may paradoxically facilitate immune evasion in lymphoma by activating the JAK2/STAT5/PD-L1 signaling axis [151]. (3) Furthermore, the JAK/STAT signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in regulating both the proliferative capacity and terminal differentiation processes of NK cells and T lymphocytes [139, 152, 153]. For example, interleukin-15 (IL-15) regulates the expansion ability and cytotoxic activity of CAR19/IL-15 NK cells against various cancer cell lines through JAK/STAT signaling [139, 154, 155]. CAR-T cell therapy sustains therapeutic persistence and exerts potent anti-tumor effects by precisely modulating JAK/STAT signaling through targeted cytokine receptor regulation [156, 157]. Collectively, targeted modulation of JAK/STAT signaling pathways holds significant therapeutic potential across multiple cancer immunotherapy modalities, including ICIs, cytokine-based treatments, and CAR-T cell therapies.

sec.title: Loss of TP53 function
sec.p: TP53 represents one of the most critical tumor suppressor genes in human malignancies, with genetic mutations or functional inactivation of TP53 being frequently observed across various cancer types. For example, the near-universal inactivation of TP53 in SCLC reveals a key biological process in this particularly aggressive malignancy [158, 159]. Furthermore, comprehensive genomic analyses have revealed that TP53 mutations occur with particularly high frequency (> 50% of cases) in several aggressive cancer types, including ESCC, TNBC, and HNSCC [160–162]. TP53 mutations often serve as initiating events in tumorigenesis and correlate strongly with tumor aggressiveness, clinical outcomes, and therapeutic sensitivity. Concurrently, these mutations modulate anti-tumor immune responses through diverse molecular mechanisms [163]. A clinically relevant example demonstrates that HCC patients harboring TP53 mutations typically show limited responsiveness to ICIs monotherapy. However, combining these treatments with targeted agents against downstream mediators of TP53 inactivation markedly enhances therapeutic outcomes. Clinical trials have reported complete response rates as high as 75% in this patient population [164].

Integrated analysis of TCGA and METABRIC datasets, combined with clinical specimen evaluation, shows that p53 signature scores and neoadjuvant chemotherapy response patterns together predict long-term outcomes in TNBC. This combined approach assesses overall prognosis, 5-year breast cancer-free survival, and the likelihood of response to immunotherapy [165, 166]. p53 inactivation in HCC triggers elevated interleukin-34 (IL-34) secretion from cancer stem cells, which subsequently promotes CD36-dependent fatty acid oxidation and facilitates the M2-polarization of TAMs. Therapeutic targeting of this IL-34-CD36 metabolic axis may potentially overcome resistance and synergize with anti-PD-1 immunotherapy in HCC treatment [164].

Molecular studies show that gain-of-function TP53 mutations directly suppress PH domain and leucine-rich repeat protein phosphatase 2 (PHLPP2) transcription. This suppression leads to hyperactivation of the AKT/eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E binding protein 1 (4EBP1)/eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) signaling cascade, ultimately enhancing PD-L1 protein translation through post-transcriptional mechanisms [167]. Comprehensive immunological analyses reveal that TP53 deficiency, either independently or in combination with MYC genomic amplification, exerts direct regulatory effects on both the tumor infiltration capacity and functional activation status of T cells [168–170].

Additionally, research indicates that p53 deletion modulates PD-L1 expression via the interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF1)/SRY-box transcription factor 10 (SOX10) axis. Futhermore, other interferon regulatory factor (IRF) family members, such as interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5) and interferon regulatory factor 9 (IRF9), as well as factors including CCL2 and Fas cell surface death receptor (FAS), have been implicated as downstream effectors of p53 in the regulation of the immune microenvironment. Although further interventional studies are needed to confirm these observations, these molecules remain potential promising therapeutic targets [171, 172].

Given the widespread immunosuppressive effects caused by p53 deficiency in the TME, scientists have explored multiple approaches to restore normal p53 function. Murine double minute 2 (MDM2) is a key negative regulator of p53, controlling both its stability and transcriptional activity. As an E3 ubiquitin ligase, MDM2 binds p53 and promotes its ubiquitination, leading to proteasomal degradation of this tumor suppressor [163, 173]. Furthermore, p53 transcriptionally activates MDM2 expression, establishing an auto-regulatory negative feedback loop that maintains p53 protein homeostasis and prevents excessive cellular responses [174]. The MDM2-p53 feedback loop is now a major focus in cancer drug development. Pharmacologically inhibiting MDM2 to reactivate tumor immunosurveillance represents a particularly promising therapeutic strategy. A clinically relevant example is ALRN-6924, an MDM2 antagonist that demonstrates therapeutic efficacy in melanoma. It activates viral mimicry pathways, upregulates pro-inflammatory tumor signature genes, and stimulates p53-dependent interferon responses. Together, these mechanisms provide a strategic approach to overcome resistance to ICIs and enhance anti-tumor immune infiltration [175]. MDM2 inhibitors significantly enhance MHC class I/II expression in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells while promoting CD8 + T-cell recruitment and activation, thereby boosting their AML-targeted cytotoxic effects [176]. Correspondingly, various p53 pathway-targeting pharmacological agents have demonstrated potent anti-leukemic activity in preclinical studies [177, 178].

In addition, local delivery of p53 mRNA or p53 protein to tumors is a promising cancer immunotherapy strategy that aims to inhibit tumor immune escape by restoring or enhancing p53 function. The p53 mRNA delivery approach involves direct introduction of TP53 gene transcripts into malignant cells to drive endogenous production of functional p53 protein. Compared to conventional gene therapy, mRNA-based delivery systems eliminate the need for sustained transgene expression while avoiding immune responses associated with viral vectors. Furthermore, immunotherapeutic approaches require only transient local p53 activation, thereby avoiding the systemic toxicity associated with traditional tumoricidal therapies [179–181]. The p53 protein delivery approach involves direct intracellular transport of synthesized p53 polypeptides, bypassing potential limitations associated with endogenous transcriptional and translational machinery. For instance, preclinical studies in TNBC models show that Pos3Aa-p53 protein crystals can restore tumor suppressor function. This treatment also induces immunogenic cell death, upregulates PD-L1, and activates type I interferon (IFN-I) pathways. Together, these effects enhance T-cell infiltration and activation, thereby potentiating anti-PD-1 therapeutic responses [182]. Modulation of the p53 signaling pathway and localized delivery of p53 mRNA/protein may exhibit synergistic therapeutic effects in distinct clinical scenarios, potentially yielding enhanced treatment outcomes in oncology applications.

sec.title: Loss of PTEN function
sec.p: PTEN loss represents one of the most prevalent oncogenic alterations spanning diverse malignancies, serving as a critical suppressor of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway hyperactivation [183, 184]. As the first cancer suppressor gene to be identified with dual-specificity phosphatase activity, PTEN negatively regulates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway via both lipid phosphatase and protein phosphatase activities [185]. Genomic aberrations in the PTEN/PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway occur in over 25% of NSCLC cases. These alterations are significantly correlated with elevated PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression [186]. Additionally, a clinical case report of advanced poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma (PDTC) demonstrated disease progression during combined immunotherapy in a PTEN-mutated patient, while subsequent incorporation of mTOR inhibitor therapy achieved 6-month disease stabilization. These findings indicate that targeted AKT pathway inhibition may overcome immunotherapy resistance in PTEN-deficient tumors [187]. In melanoma models, PTEN deficiency constitutively activates PI3K signaling and upregulates immunosuppressive cytokines such as interleukin-10 (IL-10), interleukin-2 (IL-6), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). These changes collectively inhibit T-cell infiltration and clonal expansion, thereby reducing the efficacy of PD-1 blockade [64, 188]. The FYVE, RhoGEF and PH domain-containing protein 1 (FGD1) physically interacts with PTEN to inhibit its phosphatase activity, thereby augmenting PTEN-mediated PD-L1 upregulation and consequently modulating the therapeutic response to ICIs in osteosarcoma [189]. Moreover, in the context of PTEN deficiency, pharmacological blockade of PI3Kβ signaling effectively suppressed STAT3 activation while upregulating immunostimulatory molecules, thereby enhancing anti-tumor immunity. This intervention worked synergistically with immunotherapy to enable mice that fully responded to combination therapy to exhibit immune memory [184].

In addition, PTEN exerts profound immunomodulatory effects within the TME. Secreted via transmembrane emp24 domain-containing protein 10 (TMED10) channels, extracellular PTEN binds to plexin domain-containing protein 2 (PLXDC2) receptors on macrophages. This interaction inhibits JAK2/STAT1 signaling and promotes the polarization of immunosuppressive macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype. Intratumoral delivery of PTEN protein enhances the cytotoxic activity of CD8 + T cells and NK cells, while also sensitizing tumor-bearing mice to anti-PD-1 therapy [190]. Conversely, PTEN loss in cancer cells triggers the secretion of multiple immunosuppressive cytokines, including IL-6, TGF-β, CXCL10, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 1 (CXCL1), and C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CXCL2). This cytokine milieu promotes the differentiation of CD4 + T cells into Tregs and facilitates the recruitment of MDSCs and tumor-associated neutrophils, ultimately contributing to immunotherapy resistance and poor clinical outcomes [186, 191, 192].

Analogous to p53-based approaches, targeted delivery of PTEN mRNA or recombinant protein to tumor sites demonstrates considerable therapeutic potential. Polymeric nanoparticle-mediated PTEN mRNA delivery in both PTEN-mutant melanoma and PTEN-null prostate cancer models effectively reconstituted functional PTEN expression, consequently augmenting autophagic flux and DAMPs release. Furthermore, in vivo delivery of PTEN mRNA disrupted the immunosuppressive network mediated by Tregs and MDSCs. This intervention significantly increased pro-inflammatory cytokine production and enhanced CD8 + cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration in the TME [183, 190, 193]. In addition, emerging research indicates that PTEN isoforms, especially PTENα, significantly influence both tumor development and immunotherapy efficacy. PTENα is highly expressed in multiple cancer types. It promotes immunosuppression by impairing tumor-infiltrating T lymphocyte function and facilitating immune evasion [194, 195]. These discoveries unveil novel therapeutic targets and conceptual frameworks for advancing precision immunotherapy strategies against cancers (Figs. 3 and 4).

sec.title: Influence of other oncogenic signaling pathways on cancer immunotherapy efficacy
sec.p: Multiple oncogenic signaling pathways in cancer cells intricately interconnect and dynamically interact to establish a highly complex regulatory network. Through adaptive remodeling of these signaling networks, cancer cells not only evade immune surveillance but also actively manipulate the TME, thereby significantly compromising the effectiveness of immunotherapy. For instance, both the MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways play pivotal roles in regulating cell proliferation, survival, metabolic reprogramming, and immune evasion. Beyond operating independently within cells, these pathways also extensively cross-regulate each other, forming an interconnected signaling [196, 197]. Receptor tyrosine kinases serve as the predominant upstream regulators of the MAPK/ERK cascade. Specifically, upon EGF binding, EGFR undergoes dimerization and autophosphorylation, thereby initiating the downstream RAS/MAPK/ERK signaling transduction [76]. NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations frequently exhibit an immunosuppressive microenvironment, which consequently leads to diminished clinical responses to immunotherapy. Mechanistically, EGFR mutations constitutively activate both MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT signaling cascades, leading to upregulated expression of transcription factors c-MYC and nuclear factor kappa B subunit 1 (NF-κB), respectively. These factors subsequently bind to the CD47 promoter region to enhance transcriptional activation, thereby initiating the “don’t eat me” immune evasion program. CD47 is the most critical downstream effector of EGFR activation, and pharmacological blockade of CD47 effectively reverses the suppressed phagocytic capacity of macrophages [75, 77]. Furthermore, hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway during oncolytic virotherapy significantly inhibits autophagosome biogenesis - an essential prerequisite for optimal viral replication and spread. In contrast, Activation of the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway often potentiates OV replication, an effect that is partly mediated through suppression of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascade [198, 199].

In EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients, MET amplification is a predominant resistance mechanism to EGFR-TKIs, particularly through compromising the efficacy of third-generation EGFR-TKIs designed to overcome EGFR-T790M resistance mutations. MET amplification upregulates the expression of the ectonucleotidase CD73, thereby suppressing the activation of stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling and attenuating anti-tumor immune responses in lung cancer [80]. STING is an endoplasmic reticulum-localized receptor that primarily detects aberrantly accumulated cytoplasmic DNA. Upon activation, it triggers downstream transcription factors including interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) and NF-κB, inducing the expression of IFN-I and other immunomodulatory molecules, thus initiating potent anti-tumor immune responses [200]. Furthermore, studies have demonstrated that MET signaling modulates STING 3’-UTR processing through UPF1 phosphorylation-mediated RNA stability control, consequently suppressing STING protein levels in lung cancer. This molecular mechanism drives immunosuppression characterized by diminished NK and CD8 + T cell infiltration, while concurrently promoting ICIs resistance [201]. In addition to its established functions in lung cancer, c-MET universally upregulates PD-L1 expression and actively engages in immunosuppressive signaling pathways across multiple malignancies, including HCC, glioblastoma (GBM), and gastric cancer (GC) [202–204]. Recent studies reveal that chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-Ms) targeting c-MET demonstrate significant therapeutic potential in PC. Intraperitoneally administered CAR-M-c-MET cells efficiently homed to tumor sites, selectively bound to PC cells, and potently suppressed tumor growth. Furthermore, CAR-M-c-MET cells secrete elevated levels of immune-stimulating factors compared to control macrophages and synergistically improve the efficacy of cytotoxic chemotherapy [205]. However, another evidence indicates that pharmacological MET inhibition paradoxically facilitates hepatic tumor immune evasion by suppressing T-cell-mediated anti-tumor responses [206]. The context-dependent functions of c-MET in modulating tumor immunity underscore the critical need for personalized immunotherapeutic strategies.

Similarly, NF-κB signaling exhibits a complex dual functionality in cancer immunotherapy. Pathological activation of NF-κB pathways within the TME typically enhances malignant cell proliferation, survival, and immune evasion mechanisms [207]. A comprehensive genomic analysis of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) demonstrated constitutive NF-κB inflammatory signaling activation in ~ 90% of cases. This sustained NF-κB pathway activation, coupled with persistent expression of viral RNAs and immunogenic antigens, defines the unique immune dysregulation in NPC. Notably, inhibition of NF-κB signaling effectively suppresses the proliferation of EBV-positive NPC cells [207, 208]. However, studies show that treatment-induced hyperactivation of NF-κB signaling in CRC-associated fibroblasts and immune cells enhances CD8 + T-cell chemoattractant secretion and suppresses Treg-recruiting chemokines. This shift selectively promotes effector CD8 + T-cell infiltration into tumors [209].

The reprogramming of metabolic pathways in tumor tissues has emerged as a prominent research focus in cancer immunotherapy, offering novel therapeutic strategies and promising directions for oncology treatment [108, 164, 210, 211]. Through metabolic reprogramming, including enhanced glycolysis and glutaminolysis, cancer cells acquire essential energy and biosynthetic precursors that modulate both tumor immune responses and immune cell function. This process is fundamentally regulated by dynamic alterations in multiple oncogenic signaling pathways [212, 213]. For instance, constitutive activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling axis in malignant cells enhances glucose utilization and lipogenesis, which not only promotes tumor cell survival and proliferation but also concurrently diminishes their immunogenic potential [214]. JHU083, a novel glutamine antagonist prodrug, significantly attenuates HIF-1α and c-MYC signaling phosphorylation in malignant cells while reprogramming TAMs to potentiate anti-tumor immunity [215]. Intriguingly, pharmacological glutamine inhibition disrupts both oxidative phosphorylation and glycolytic pathways in tumor cells, inducing hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, and nutrient deprivation. Remarkably, effector T cells adapt to glutamine restriction by enhancing mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and acquiring a long-lived, hyperactivated phenotypic state [215, 216]. This metabolic divergence establishes an ideal therapeutic window for immunotherapeutic interventions. Furthermore, the Hippo pathway effectors YAP/TAZ directly induce glucose transporter 3 (GLUT3) expression and upregulate glycolytic regulators including hexokinase 2 (HK2) and 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-biphosphatase 3 (PFKFB3) via Hedgehog signaling activation, consequently potentiating glycolytic flux in tumor cells [217, 218]. Additionally, YAP/TAZ activation promotes glutamine metabolic reprogramming in breast cancer through transcriptional upregulation of solute carrier family 1 member 5 (SLC1A5) and glutaminase (GLS), two critical mediators of glutamine transport and catabolism [219].
In summary, investigating these critical signaling pathways is anticipated to yield novel therapeutic breakthroughs and advance precision immunotherapy strategies for cancer treatment (Fig. 5).

sec.title: Future directions and perspectives on clinical translation
sec.p: Cancer immunotherapy has brought new hope to patients, yet still faces many challenges. Integrating oncogenic signaling pathways into treatment strategies may help overcome current limitations and open new avenues for progress.

First, it is critical to investigate the mechanisms through which interactive oncogenic signaling networks mediate immunotherapy resistance. Advances in single-cell and spatial multi-omics technologies facilitate the mapping of signaling network interactions among diverse tumor cell subpopulations, providing a theoretical basis for multi-target combination therapies against complex drug resistance mechanisms [220, 221]. Secondly, developing precise biomarkers is critical for patient stratification and personalized therapy. Currently, predicting immunotherapy efficacy using methods like PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden is challenged by heterogeneity, threshold variability, and other limitations. Research has revealed that serine/threonine kinase 11 (STK11) deficiency drives alterations in the STING/IFN-I pathway. This dysregulation serves as a biomarker for predicting primary resistance or response to immunotherapy, facilitating patient stratification in clinical trials [222]. On this basis, monitoring changes in pathway-related genes by detecting ctDNA in liquid biopsy samples facilitates the prediction of treatment efficacy and enables timely adjustments to therapeutic strategies [223]. Finally, promoting the clinical translation of targeted pathway and immunotherapy combinations remains a critical future direction. Currently, numerous modulators targeting various pathways are in early-stage research or clinical development. Future clinical trials should prioritize testing in specific patient populations defined by reliable biomarkers. Additionally, the integration of signaling pathway modulators with novel therapeutic modalities, such as adoptive cell therapy and tumor vaccines, holds broad promise. For example, JAK/STAT pathway modulators can be employed to regulate the differentiation state of CAR-T cells, thereby enhancing their anti-tumor efficacy [157, 224, 225].

In summary, the translation of fundamental research findings into clinical practice demands a concerted multidisciplinary effort. Through an enhanced comprehension of oncogenic signaling networks and the rational design of combination therapies, we can progressively address the challenge of immune resistance, ultimately extending durable clinical benefits to a greater number of cancer patients.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Distinct from conventional interventions like surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, cancer immunotherapy primarily harnesses and enhances immune system functionality. This approach employs ICIs, immune cell engineering, tumor vaccines, and other modalities to facilitate immune-mediated tumor recognition and elimination [60]. However, malignant cells frequently dysregulate critical signaling pathways to enhance their survival and evade immune surveillance. Additionally, tumors actively secrete immunosuppressive mediators including TGF-β and IL-10, which impair immune cell function and consequently constrain the efficacy of immunotherapeutic approaches [20, 226]. Targeted modulators of oncogenic signaling pathways show great potential for improving cancer immunotherapy. When used synergistically with conventional approaches such as ICIs and adoptive cell therapy, these modulators may lead to substantially better clinical outcomes. Intervening signaling pathways during cancer immunotherapy aims to (1) increase immune cell activity: Malignant cells suppress T-cell activation through dysregulation of multiple signaling pathways, thereby promoting tumor survival and immunotherapy resistance. Notably, the PI3K/AKT signaling axis plays a pivotal role in mediating both cancer cell proliferation and immune evasion. Pharmacological inhibition of PI3K/AKT signaling not only potentiates T-cell function but also diminishes tumor immune escape mechanisms. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that PI3K inhibitors significantly enhance the therapeutic efficacy of both ICIs and adoptive T-cell therapies [227, 228]. (2) reversing the immunosuppressive TME: Immunosuppressive mediators frequently inhibit immune cells within the TME, impairing their ability to effectively identify and eliminate malignant cells. TGF-β serves as a pivotal regulator of tumor immune evasion, suppressing anti-tumor immunity while fostering immune tolerance. Therapeutic targeting of TGF-β signaling through specific inhibitors or modulators can counteract this immunosuppression and restore immune-mediated tumor recognition and destruction [229, 230]. (3) disruption of immune tolerance mechanisms: Malignant cells actively modulate immunosuppressive cell populations including Tregs, MDSCs, and TAMs through intercellular signaling networks to evade immune surveillance. Therapeutic targeting of immune evasion can reinstate immune competence and significantly enhance immunotherapy efficacy [66, 164, 186]. (4) remodeling the TME: Tumor cells exploit hypoxic and acidic conditions within the TME to stimulate immunosuppressive cytokine production, establishing an immune-privileged niche that protects them from immune cell-mediated destruction. Notably, the NF-κB signaling pathway serves as a central regulator of immune responses, inflammatory processes, and cellular survival mechanisms in the TME. In addition, HIF-1α pathway activation under tumor hypoxia facilitates malignant cell adaptation while simultaneously suppressing anti-tumor immunity. Therapeutic targeting of both NF-κB and HIF-1α signaling pathways may effectively remodel the TME to favor immune cell activation and function [72, 207]. The strategic integration of oncogenic signaling pathway modulators with immunotherapy represents a transformative approach for precision medicine. Given the heterogeneous genetic alterations and signaling dysregulation across cancer types, personalized combination therapies based on molecular profiling are expected to substantially enhance immunotherapeutic outcomes [231].

In addition, while oncogenic signaling pathway modulators show considerable promise in enhancing immunotherapy, their clinical translation still encounters several challenges. Firstly, modulators targeting oncogenic signaling pathways may inadvertently disrupt normal cellular and immune functions, potentially causing adverse effects. This underscores the need for more precise drug development and tailored therapeutic approaches to minimize off-target toxicity [232]. Secondly, the intrinsic heterogeneity of malignant cells enables them to develop resistance through adaptive signaling pathway mutations and reprogramming. Implementing combinatorial approaches with multiple targeted agents and immunotherapies may provide an effective strategy to circumvent such resistance mechanisms [3, 66, 75]. Finally, while several signaling pathway modulators have entered clinical use, their synergistic efficacy when combined with immunotherapy requires further validation through extensive multicenter clinical trials. In summary, oncogenic signaling pathway modulators hold tremendous promise for enhancing cancer immunotherapy. Through targeting immune evasion mechanisms, potentiating immune cell functionality, and reprogramming the TME, these modulators can substantially augment immunotherapeutic efficacy. Nevertheless, key challenges including treatment safety, acquired resistance, and the refinement of personalized combination strategies remain critical priorities for future investigation.
